MR. MARCEAU-OBJECTION TO STATEMENT OF MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege in connection with a statement made yesterday evening by the hon. member for Port-neuf (Mr. Godin).
As recorded in Hansard at page 1441, the hon. member stated, and I quote:
Hon. members know how sensitive I am and incapable of expressing malevolent views of making charges.
This might be the only time he said anything true since the rest of his speech is made up of slanderous and inexcusable charges directed against the bar association and myself.
At the end of his speech, the hon. member for Portneuf made a reference to a speeding charge laid against him and mentioning the member for Lapointe he stated the following:
At the same time, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) a Liberal member, went through a 30 mile an hour zone at 100 miles an hour. He simply had to pay $50 fine. Well if politics do not come into play in cases like that, I certainly would like to know.
I should like to say to the hon. member for Portneuf and to other members of this House that our private lives have nothing to do with our proceedings and that hon. members are in no way interested in learning about them.
The charge laid by the hon. member for Portneuf is entirely inaccurate and the circumstances under which he was fined $250 are entirely different from those in my case. I wish to say to the hon. member that such charges made in the absence of the person concerned indicate a narrow-mindedness about which I will say no more.
I do not associate all Ralliement creditiste members with such statements, because I have the pleasure of knowing several of them who are honest and charming people. I must say, none the less, that the hon. member for Portneuf disappoints me greatly when he refers to such things. I hope he will withdraw his remarks in due time if he wants us to remain friends.

The urgent circumstances are as follows: The almost universal opposition in the media and from individuals to the provisions of Bill C-190 makes it clear that Canadians take the strongest objection to any attempt to restrict the authority of the Auditor General. Nevertheless, the continuance of the bill on the order paper in its present form constitutes an attempt to intimidate and harass the Auditor General in the discharge of his duties and to inhibit his examination of such government spending as the substantial increase in costs alleged in respect of the destroyer construction program.

subtopic: CANADIAN TV-CUTTING OF FILMS
CANADIAN TV-CUTTING OF FILMS
speechtext:
1.	How many films shown on Canadian TV in the years 1969 and 1970 were cut in length from the original film?
2.	What was the average amount of time the films were cut when shown on Canadian television?
3.	Has CRTC done any research into the cutting of the films shown on television and, if so, what research has been done and is the cutting of the film considered to be an unfair or deceptive practice to the public?

subtopic: CANADIAN TV-CUTTING OF FILMS
speechtext:
1. I am
informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that the CBC keeps no record of the films or other programs cut in length for presentation on television. Complete film or tape programs may be cut in length for one or more of the following reasons: (a) In the case of a television series produced in North America, the program length may have to be cut very slightly in order to accommodate commercial messages, institutional announcements, or program promotional items, (b) Film programs produced in Europe that are not specifically tailored to
North American requirements may have to be shortened slightly because the television projection rate in North America is 4% slower than in Europe, (c) Feature films produced for theatrical release rarely accord with the required program length. Usually features have to be edited to fit the program time slot available, although occasionally they are short enough to be presented in their original form, (d) Film or tape programs that contain unredeemed violence, illegal visual or sound content, or in which there is extreme exploitation of the emotions, are cut by the minimum amount necessary, where these programs are otherwise desirable.
In the case of television series, wherever possible the cuts are made where there is no dialogue, and in every case a conscientious attempt is made to respect the integrity of the original production or story line. In the editing of features, the original concept and balance are preserved as much as possible. Films regarded as "classics", or those produced by acknowledged masters of the cinema, are invariably either presented intact or not at all. In the preparation of a magazine type program a short segment illustrating a particular topic is sometimes taken from a longer film.
2.	I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: (a) On North American television series where cutting is necessary, approximately 40 seconds in a half-hour program and approximately 50 seconds in programs lasting an hour or longer, (b) Feature films scheduled at the end of the broadcast day are usually allowed to run out without any cuts. Those scheduled earlier, when the timing is more inflexible, are edited by the amount of time necessary to enable them to fit the time period available. Typically, this could run between five and twenty-five minutes.
3.	I am informed by the Canadian Radio Television Commission that the CRTC has not conducted any special research on this matter. Through its monitoring activities, the study of station logs, and its general surveillance of program practice, the Broadcast Programs Branch of the CRTC is familiar with the fact that episodes of television series produced outside Canada are sometimes cut by small amounts to accommodate advertising material. Feature length films, not made originally for television, frequently are cut to fit the more rigid time schedule of television. The manner in which the editing is done is extremely important so that the deletions do not distort or destroy the dramatic sequence of events in the original. But unfortunately the Commission has been unable to do any research on the subject.

speechtext: How many companies and businesses have restricted their expansion of operation as a result of the government's austerity and anti-inflation programme?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bruce Howard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: RESTRICTION OF EXPANSION DUE TO GOVERNMENT'S AUSTERITY AND ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Investment decisions by companies are normally made in the light of anticipated growth in market demand and rate or return on the investment. One purpose of the government's anti-inflationary program is to hold down costs thus enabling producers to become internationally competitive with resulting benefits in terms of sales growth and improved returns on investment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It has to do with the United Nations General Assembly resolution which called for the unconditional resumption of the Middle East talks and which was passed with the United States voting against the resolution. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN ABSTENTION IN VOTE ON RESOLUTION CALLING FOR RESUMPTION OF MIDDLE EAST PEACE TALKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the right hon. member will know if he followed the debate very closely, that we voted with Israel on a motion proposed by the Latin American countries which was satisfactory to Israel. We voted with them and that motion was defeated. Then came the motion that had been proposed by the Afro-Asian bloc which we had been trying, not with too much success but with some success, to have modified in such a form that it might have been acceptable to us. We did not succeed and therefore we abstained.

subtopic: CANADIAN ABSTENTION IN VOTE ON RESOLUTION CALLING FOR RESUMPTION OF MIDDLE EAST PEACE TALKS

subtopic: CANADIAN ABSTENTION IN VOTE ON RESOLUTION CALLING FOR RESUMPTION OF MIDDLE EAST PEACE TALKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that is quite clear. We wanted that motion to be fully consonant with resolution 242 of the Security Council. Since it was not, we abstained.

speechtext: Has the minister since received criticism from various Jewish organizations across Canada for having maintained a position of neutrality at a time when Israel needed Canada's help?

speechtext: We had commendation from them for supporting the motion supported by Israel. We protested very strongly against the inopportuneness of the debate itself which we felt, and which I still feel did not advance very much the cause of peace in the Middle East.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night I had just begun giving my reasons for believing that the amendment proposed to Bill C-181 should be defeated.
It is true that this bill may adversely affect the civil liberties of many people in the province of Quebec. This is unfortunate; it has always been the case when such things take place. Only a few days ago the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Douglas) spoke very eloquently on this theme. He gave as an example the situation of Japanese Canadians during the war and what had taken place on the west coast. He reminded us that these people had been interned and that after the war it was found that not one case could be shown of a Japanese Canadian being guilty of an offence against the war effort. We all agree with this and know it to be true. What the leader of the NDP neglected to point out, however, was that when this action took place, Canada was in danger-and when the country itself is in danger civil liberties must be forgotten to some extent.
What was done was most unfortunate. Certainly it was a dark day in the pages of Canadian history when these most loyal Canadian Japanese were interned. But I would impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, and upon all members of the House that we cannot gamble with the safety of 22 million Canadians at the present time by thinking about civil liberties when they effect only relatively few people. Of course, as I say, it is unfortunate. I know this Parliament and the provincial legislatures will do everything possible to see that civil liberties are not unduly interfered with. But Canada is too great a nation to allow the safety and the future of 22 million people to be endangered because of arguments based on the fact that up to the moment some 400 people have been jailed and not charged.
I would remind my friends to the left of this chamber who have opposed this legislation at every opportunity, that members of the FLQ are not a bunch of Sunday school teachers; they do not go to church every Sunday. They are people who have condoned bombing and murder. This, of course, is not in accordance with the way we live here in Canada. I point out too, that the vast majority of the people of Canada agree with what the government has done, and they agree with what the government is attempting to do now in replacing the War Measures Act by legislation which is at least not quite so trying.
All hon. members have to do is read their mail to find out that when the War Measures Act was passed in the first place, there were probably a thousand Communists in Canada opposed to it, a thousand supporters of the FLQ, 16 members of the New Democratic Party and one Tory. And 22 million Canadians were in favour of it. We cannot afford in any circumstances to gamble with the freedom of those 22 million Canadians. It is, of course, unfortunate that some people who may not be as guilty as the police have suggested they are, should be put in jail. It may take a few days or it may take a month before they come to trial, but eventually they will have their day in court.
In closing, I express the hope that hon. members to my left will stop this nonsense of bringing in amendments every hour and calling for a vote every day. We have important things to do in this Parliament. There are senior citizens who deserve a little better treatment in the form of increased pensions. Our veterans need higher pensions and allowances. There are many other tasks which remain to be done. Today the government is attempting to remove some of the hardship of the War Measures Act, and I ask hon. members to my left to show the dignity which their constituents expect them to use in this hallowed chamber and let us get on with the business of making Canada a better place for its citizens to live in.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were exclamations on the government side when I rose. However, I wish to point out that I have certainly not taken too much of the time of the House during this debate, since this is the first time that I speak to the subject. I listened patiently to the other hon. members and I hope that my colleagues will show me the same consideration.
We have things to say on this bill. Indeed, we shall introduce an amendment, if not several. We have not been able to do so until now because the procedure allows the other opposition parties to introduce as many amendments as they wish. As a consequence, the Rallie-ment creditiste could not participate in the debate to the same extent as the official opposition party or the New Democratic Party with their numerous amendments.
Mr. Speaker, we have now reached third reading of Bill C-181, which aims at replacing the War Measures Act invoked after the October events.
We supported the government then because we had no alternative in the circumstances. The government had promised to introduce in the House, as soon as possible, legislation to maintain public order in the event of circumstances similar to those we have just experienced.
We were therefore expecting permanent legislation which would have applied to the whole nation from Halifax to Vancouver.
We wanted a legislation with clear definitions and precise enforcement clauses. We are obliged to confess that, unfortunately, this is not the case and that our hopes did not materialize.
After the first reading of the bill, we carefully considered the government proposals because we hoped to use the study in committee of the whole as a means to oblige the government to rectify some of the monstrosities contained in its bill. However, this did not happen because the government group, behind its absolute majority, seemed to take a cunning delight in defeating with complacency all the amendments which could have improved certain parts of the bill.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel) .1
Everything was turned down flat, except for a few insignificant words. I listened and watched these developments and I did not see any reason even to vote because of the uselessness of these arguments since the government was determined to accept no change.
If I rise to speak today, it is not because I feel that I could make the government more congenial in view of the fact that the word was passed and orders will be fully and blindly obeyed as usual.
My only purpose is to reveal to the people the tactics used by the government to make us vote for Bill C-181, which we opposed in its present form, because it is not national in scope; it is only temporary and applies only to Quebec. Furthermore, it is not clear and it could undermine the very foundation of our legal system.
As members of the Canadian Parliament, the legislation we pass must be national in scope. We notice that this bill deals only with the FLQ movement in Quebec as if difficulties could erupt and FLQ demonstrations could take place only in Quebec.
However, we already have evidence to the contrary. Certainly all the provinces are not immune from the FLQ ideology since some people have already been arrested even in Ontario on parliament hill, in front of the peace tower.
I have seen with my own eyes signs bearing the words FLQ. We have seen them in British Colombia and even in England where one FLQ member just committed suicide.
Mr. Speaker, that one at least did not agree with the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on capital punishment.
In order to reach the Front de Liberation du Quebec, would it not have been more logical and particularly more realistic to propose measures to protect public order in Canada in general? Is it to be acknowledged that the word "Canada" excludes the province of Quebec? Those who drafted the measure probably had something against Quebec. They wanted all Canada to see that province explicitely named in a law.
Is this not simply discrimination? I cannot really find the spirit which moved the government to use such a procedure. On certain days, we would very much like to know what goes on in the mind of the right hon. Prime Minister. Besides, many on the government side ask themselves the same question. He appears to us as an elusive man with a thousand contradictions. At times, he frightens us.
Indeed, now he appears as the untiring protector of the laws of Quebec, now he multiplies opportunities and reasons to further interfere with jurisdictions previously reserved exclusively to the provinces.
I realized that when I heard him answer the hon. Leader of the Oppositon (Mr. Stanfield) in connection with the bill before us. The Leader of the Opposition, as recorded on page 1359 of Hansard, was asking whether the Prime Minister was prepared to support a provision for an independent review in the public order bill.
November 25, 1970

The Prime Minister then answered, and I quote:
I submit that the amendment proposed by the opposition along the lines of establishing such a commission would precisely be doing that, seeking confrontation with the province of Quebec in a matter of its jurisdiction-
What does the Prime Minister do with the jurisdiction of Quebec-which he has just cherished-in the areas of health, education and culture?
Assistance given by the federal government will be used as an excuse, but Quebeckers know that through taxes levied by the federal government they pay this so-called assistance ten times over.
I mention this because I consider that the causes which force the government to present this bill do not originate only in reprehensible acts by some members of the FLQ. It is therefore our duty, in our capacity as elected representatives of the people, to scrutinize this matter more exhaustively. I will add that it is up to this government to make a serious examination of its conscience, in order to determine whether its attitude towards the province of Quebec is not the main reason behind the dissatisfaction which is evident in that province.
Since the last general election, the Liberal government is giving the impression that it is doing its gest to provoke Quebeckers and keep them in line through fear.
Under the former Prime Minister, there had been a glimpse of hope for Quebec to recover its autonomy. In fact, the former Prime Minister had promised to eliminate all joint programs and to transfer back to the Quebec government all the taxation fields which had been temporarily granted to the federal government during the last war.
The Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson then recognized that Quebec was not a province like the others and this never prevented it from being one of the best partners in Confederation. But this dream was too good for Quebeckers, too expensive for Ottawa and too dangerous for high finance. This is why Mr. Pearson was obliged to leave his place to another not so diplomatic Prime Minister.
Unfortunately, once more it had to be a French Canadian who would take care of the dirty job of restraining Quebec's noble aspirations.
And of all contradictions, this Prime Minister is still pretending that Quebec is and must be a province like the others, like all English-speaking provinces.
In my opinion, the roots of the evil are this inflexible obstination. If you add to this an unbearable economic situation at all levels because of the double taxation, you know why there are so many rebels in Quebec.
We are against this bill because its application is only temporary. In fact, it will expire in April 1971 as if the government were sure that at that date all the FLQ members will have been eliminated or will have become Liberal supporters.
The War Measures Act was temporary. Now, we replace it with another temporary legislation. When shall we have a permanent legislation? Finally, we are against
Public Order Act, 1970
this bill because there is nothing clear, no accurate definition in it.
We still have to ask the government what they mean by "unlawful association" and that is why, seconded by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne), I move the following amendment:
That Bill C-181 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of reconsidering clause 3 as amended concerning the definition of the unlawful association.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
We fear that this measure will be a blow to the basic principles of our legal system. So far, in the province of Quebec, the accused was deemed to be innocent as long as the Crown had not demonstrated that he was guilty. If Bill C-181 is passed, the accused in Quebec-and in Quebec only-will be deemed to be guilty as long as he has not demonstrated himself that he is innocent.
I consider this "overthrow" of our jurisprudence to be just as frightening as the overthrow of our system of government by an association of reactionary citizens. The whole thing is carried out in a very hush-hush fashion and this will make it even more harmful to Quebecers. It is just another gimmick designed to pump some more money into lawyers' pockets and to starve to death those indicted by the state.
Let us stop asking ourselves why there are so many rebels in Quebec. Oh, they may not all be revolutionaries ready to take up arms, but revolt lies deep in their hearts, and that is even worse.
Mr. Speaker, are those people solely responsible? I say no, because too often they have been betrayed by the members they elected. The Quebec people are a peaceful people; all they want is the right to lead their own life in Canada, not the kind of life dictated to them by the central government.
We know public order demands that the law be respected, and I am all for it. But, in return, the government must respect the rights of every individual. To live its own life fully Quebec needs all its financial resources. You may rest assured that with those resources and the return of the taxing powers the federal government sneaked away from it, Quebec will no longer come begging to Ottawa: it can then live happily, just like Ontario and the other Western provinces.
All this to say that Bill C-181 will not solve the case of the FLQ or bring peace back to Quebec.
The law will make it possible to put a few in jail, but most will go free. More than anybody else, I hope that the people will regain confidence in our institutions. It is the only way to restore peace.
I urge the government to give up the idea of resorting to repression and to act more sensibly. We are no longer living in the age of caves and ghettos, but in the age of dialogue and negotiation.
The reign of dictators is over and it is useless to try to return to those historical times. We must go back to the true democracy of government by the people and for the people.

Public Order Act, 1970
Finance must be at man's service. Man must not be the slave of our rotten and outmoded financial system. We have been earnestly fighting here for years in the hope of bringing to reason government members who have always been the docile servants of big finance.
Once more, we urge them to help all workers, farmers, fathers, young people who are expecting from government members the opportunity to live a full life in their country, Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise merely for the purpose of saying that the amendment asks that Bill C-181 be not read a third time but be referred back to Committee of the Whole for the purpose of considering the definition of "unlawful association" contained in clause 3 thereof. We have serious reservations about the terms of clause 3. Our reservations are not those expressed by the hon. member who has just spoken. He is under the impression that this clause applies only to the province of Quebec. We take it to mean that it applies throughout Canada. The latter part of clause 3, as amended, beginning at line 9, reads as follows:
-or substantially the same governmental change within Canada with respect to the province of Quebec or its relationship to Canada as that advocated by the said le Front de Liberation du Quebec, is declared to be an unlawful association.
While we do not follow the logic of the member of the Ralliement Creditiste who has just spoken, nevertheless we think changes ought to be made to clause 3. We have taken particular objection, as we have said on other occasions, to the word "advocates". Clause 3 speaks of any group of persons or association that advocates the use of force. The term "advocates" is so broad that it could even cover an abstract, theoretical discussion of the necessity of using force in order to bring about separation of the province of Quebec from our confederation. We have felt all along that a term such as "incites" would be more specific and more restrictive.
For this reason we are inclined to support this amendment to send the bill back to the committee, because we think that clause 3 ought to be reviewed. Nevertheless, our reasons for so doing are not similar to those expressed by the previous speaker.

Mr. Speaker, without repeating the arguments I put before the House yesterday afternoon with regard to the whole process of making an association unlawful under the terms of the bill, while not agreeing with all the reasons put forward by the hon. member I believe that this clause is the nub of the legislation and is what makes it so reprehensible. Neither the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) nor the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has yet clearly indicated to the House or the country what the FL.Q stands for or how, in aE justice, this kind of legislation will work effectively in

the province of Quebec or anywhere else. Because of that, I am led to support this amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even if I have examined the amendment to clause 3, there is stiU enough doubt in my mind for me to support the amendment that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole.
I understand, as stated by the previous speaker, that the bill is applicable, according to its first draft, throughout Canada. However, the amendment, passed in the committee of the whole concerning page 3, fine 8, after the word "Canada" where the following words are added: "with respect to the Province of Quebec or its relationship to Canada,", shall necessarily be included in clause 3. We should therefore logically refer the bill, as provided in the amendment, to the committee of the whole for thorough consideration and to enable it to give a more detailed definition of the terms "any association of Quebec."
I think it might be advisable to take a closer look at the possibility of widening the scope of this clause to provide for a similar situation eventually arising in another province of Canada.
The older among us well remember the famous Cha-loult trial which took place during World War II. This good man, a member of the Quebec legislative assembly, had had the courage to express strong nationalistic opinions at a political meeting during the war. And under legislation which was not clear enough he was charged, brought to court, forced to defend himself, to secure the services of top notch lawyers, although he himself was a very famous one, in order to estabhsh beyond doubt in court that he was not a revolutionary, that he had not intended inacting the population to say no to the requests of the government concerning the defence of freedom outside Canada.
He had simply wanted, as a good Canadian, to speak a language that had been heard quite often during the electoral campaigns of 1924, 1925, 1930, 1935 and 1939, to the effect that not a single French Canadian would ever be mobilized. He had simply repeated remarks which had been used quite often to invite the people of Quebec to place their confidence in a certain party.
I remember that I followed this trial with the greatest interest and this memory has burnt into my mind.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I am just wondering how this legislation will be interpreted when it will have to be enforced. Will it be possible, in some cases, to accuse a person who has good intentions, but may be more of a nationalist than others, and therefore may use more direct and more violent words? Would it then be possible, under clause 3 of the bill, under some pretext, to charge that person of inciting others to use force or commit a crime to reach some goals?
I feel that in the interest of the whole of Canada and also in the interest of justice itself, we should take the
November 25, 1970

trouble, as parliamentarians and responsible people, to reconsider this clause, taking into account the amendment that has just been moved.
When the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) rose a few minutes ago, I was very upset to note that some members were distressed. Yet, we are in parliament. If we take a close look at the word parliament, we find that it means a place where one can speak. If in our democratic parliamentary system, we have reached the point where it is a negative gesture aimed at extending the debate and at embarrassing the government when somebody rises to express his view-thus to speak-I wonder where we are heading for.
Being fully aware of the dignity and the ability of the member for Roberval, I am convinced that, like all other members, he does not wish to extend the debate deliberately.
As I was among responsible people, I have been accustomed, from a very early age, to assuming my responsibilities. I consider that one should play when it is time to play and work when it is time to work. Indeed, one should take things seriously when it is time to do so.
It is therefore our duty to review the clause thoughtfully, in an effort to improve it, to bring it more into line with our traditions and to give more protection to the freedom of those, still in a very great majority in Canada and particularly in Quebec, who are imbued with the principle of respect for the freedom of others.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize, at the beginning of my speech, the realism, the clarity and the lucidity of the remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), when the amendment before us was introduced. In my opinion, he made the most remarkable speech that we have heard since we started discussing the War Measures Act, for he pointed out that it was essential to proceed methodically and without too much haste in passing legislation which can rightly be applied not only today, but also in the month of April, or later if necessary.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The urgency of this emergency measure should not overly alarm us because if, in fact, with all the strengh and force of the war measures, the police are not bright enough to look in closets to find the kidnappers, it is not the passage of this emergency act that will ensure greater success. There is therefore no urgency to pass this emergency act.
However we can take this opportunity to adopt a measure which might be quite useful to the government when it decides to introduce permanent legislation on the matter.
In today's Le Devoir may be found an article by Karl Lewitt, associate professor of economics at McGill University, which I would like to quote:
Should I remind you that invoking the War Measures Act has neither saved the life of Pierre Laporte nor obtained the release of James Cross nor hastened the arrest of the abductors and
Public Order Act, 1970
murderers; this Act was not needed to move the RCMP and the army into Montreal, nor to deliver all the warrants required under the Criminal Code, nor to search everywhere and question all suspects. Still we are entitled to know exactly why the War Measures Act was invoked. Whatever the Prime Minister may say, those reasons remain inconspicuous.
Of all the more serious arguments handed out by government leaders when the country became panic-stricken, there was this "apprehended insurrection" and "wearing away of the people's will in Quebec". No evidence has yet been given to support either of these allegations; therefore, we have to take their word for it. And this brings us back to question the reliability, the integrity and the motivations of the politicians concerned.
Therefore, this is only a matter of opinion; the authorities did not leave us much choice.
When we, during the most tragical events of October, were called upon to pass the War Measures Act, we then took the word of the government and its leader, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who said he had every reason to believe that the War Measures Act was necessary.
More than one month has gone by and we are now inclined to believe that his reasons were not justified.
This is why, now that we are going to pass a legislation which aims at putting an end to violence, we must not give any chance to those responsible for violence or those who would be tempted to use it.
With the situation prevailing in Canada, and especially in Quebec, we cannot afford to insult Quebecers, and this is what will happen if clause 3, as amended Monday, is left in the act.
Clause 3, which defines the illegal association, may be interpreted in numerous ways, as I mentioned last Monday. My colleague the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) just mentioned, with concrete examples to support it, that the government could even go as far as jailing all those who would fail to please them, if they were to abuse their power.
This is what we want to prevent. We must avoid by all means giving to those who are ready to resort to violence-but who have not yet done so-new motives to use violent means. This is why we must quietly and reasonably attempt to embody in equitable legislation ways and means to put an end to violent confrontations.
Mr. Speaker, we are being told that violence is not the prerogative of the province of Quebec but the government went as far as to accept, Monday last, an amendment designed to pinpoint the type of offence covered by the bill, namely "Canada with respect to the province of Quebec or its relationship to Canada". In my view, it is quite clear that this provision is only designed to establish whether the FLQ acted in Canada or not. If the FLQ acted in Canada, then let us pass an act that applies to Canada. To my mind, the argument is very simple.
By making that distinction, making that reservation in Clause 3 of the bill, and the preamble, it is implicitly recognized that the act applies only to Quebec. One of the objectives of the FLQ is recognized in part. I think we must pass an act that applies throughout Canada, because by saying that the FLQ exists not in Canada, but in Quebec, we recognize the separation of Quebec. Let us
1482	__________COMMONS DEBATES_____________________November 25, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
admit one of two things: that the possibility of the secession of Quebec is imminent, or that the FLQ is acting in Canada. That is the alternative facing the government when it persists in stating specifically that it is meant for Quebec.
The more so as Clause 3 is vague in many regards, namely where it stipulates, and I quote:
-in accomplishing the same or substantially the same governmental change-
Well, Mr. Speaker, this point has to be cleared up.
In Quebec, on April 29, 700,000 people voted PQ. If we were to convict people because of their aims, we would have quite an extraordinary case of abuse which could lead the government to take away all possibilities of constitutional emancipation for Quebec.
We must therefore take that into consideration, weigh each word and evaluate properly the scope of the clauses of this act to provide emergency powers.
Mr. Speaker, in Quebec, not so long ago, the leader of a party nearly still-born, the Christian Nationalist Party, was stealing paintings or had them stolen on the ground that christianism must be saveguarded in Quebec. It is quite laudable to want the expansion of christianism, the protection of religion and confessionality in schools, but if we resort to stealing and to violence to attain such a purpose, this is inadmissible, no matter how good the purpose can be.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
This is why, when we say that the movement or the association become unlawful, provided they seek the same ends as the FLQ, we allow abuse of power. And when we know that our government at the present time is very close to dictatorship, we do fear that this insignificant emergency legislation might be used in order to control Quebec once and for all and to prevent its true emancipation and development.
Therefore there are truly several reasons for requesting a more complete and more responsible study of clause 3. It is not because we have to put an immediate end to terrorist activities in Canada that we should pass meaningless legislation.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, the War Measures Act is still in effect and it is a lot more efficient than the bill under consideration. If we do not succeed in arresting the offenders under the War Measures Act, what would be the use of a much less efficient legislation. All the more so, Mr. Speaker, since trouble is not restricted to Quebec. My colleague, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), has just told us about what happened in the House last year when a group of young ladies or women tied down to their seats came here to disrupt order. As far as I know, they were not from Quebec. On the contrary, most of them came from the other end of the country, which shows that trouble can erupt anywhere. I do not want to impute motives to anyone but I wonder what would happen had these ladies been from Quebec.

Others besides Quebeckers have also been the source of trouble. As an example I will mention what happened at Sir George Williams University in Montreal where damages amounted to several million dollars. Once again, those involved were not necessarily Quebeckers, members of the FLQ.
Therefore, this emergency act should enable to determine which organizations it is essential to treat rigorously in order to check any violence, regardless of its goals. Clause 3 implies, as I said Monday, that if an association uses force and violence to strengthen Canadian federalism, it would pursue a commendable goal, since clause 3 specifies that it is necessary that the goal of the indicted association be identical with that of the FLQ. There is clearly something irrational in that clause. That is why I strongly and whole-heartedly support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Roberval.

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief and precise in my remarks, I hope, concerning the object of the amendment moved by my friends of the Ralliement Creditiste. They suggest in the wording of their amendment that clause 3 restricts the application of this act to the province of Quebec. They refer to words which were added a few days ago, in committee, to clause 3, namely those concerning the province of Quebec or its relationship to Canada. Those words appeared and still appear in the second paragraph of the preamble. They do not restrict geographically the implementation of the act, but they specify the definition of the FLQ with regard to its aims and objectives.
As a further precision, this legislation will apply throughout Canada. Its application will not be geographically restricted to Quebec. The law will be applicable by the Attorney general of Ontario, by the Quebec Minister of Justice or by the Attorney general of British Columbia, against the FLQ or any other association with the same objectives as the FLQ, namely the overthrowing by force or by crime of the Quebec government in relation to the rest of Canada.
The field of application of this legislation is not limited to Quebec but is aimed at the FLQ. This is a most specific legislation. As the member for Champlain (M. Matte) said, the government will have to look more fully into the problem of violence or of the use of force in our society.
I am trying to prove to the satisfaction of my friends opposite that the amendment recently adopted has brought about no essential change. I explained that point to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan The Islands (Mr. Douglas), to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). They were under the impression that clause 3 was not clear enough as concerns the aims and objectives of the FLQ.
Therefore, to clear up the matter, I thought advisable to add the words in the preambule. I believe that was unnecessary, since under the Interpretation Act, the preamble is included in the interpretation of other parts of the statute.
November 25, 1970

I should like to refer the house to section 12 of the Interpretation Act, contained in the 1967-68 Statutes of Canada. It reads as follows:
The preamble of an enactment shall be read as a part thereof Intended to assist in explaining its purport and object.
Therefore, the act is clear, even without the amendment made at the suggestion of the hon. member for York South. The legislation had to be clarified. To satisfy the claims of the hon. member, I proposed the addition of those words, and I want to give the mover of this amendment the assurance that I have in no way changed the essence of his proposal. It is simply a question of clarification.
To make myself clear about the advice I get from the legal advisers in the Department of Justice, I say again that, of course, this legislation will apply all over Canada. It is aimed at the FLQ, and this, throughout Canada.
I recognize that the hon. members on the other side may have experienced some interpretation problems, but I want them to be sure of the good faith of the government as regards this amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I on behalf of the official opposition, make it very clear at the outset that we reject the amendment that has been proposed. I should like to explain why we reject it. Clause 3, as amended, deals primarily with the organization known as le Front de Liberation du Quebec. It is obvious from any of the facts about this organization that have come to our attention that it fits all the elements of what has become the twentieth century classic terrorist organization. For one thing, it does not hold public meetings; its work is clandestine. As far as anybody is aware, there are no doves in this organization and no philosophers advocating peaceful means. Its arguments are conducted at the point of a gun used against people whose hands are tied behind their backs. It uses terror tactics purely and simply. It steals dynamite to use the same. It steals guns to use the same. It preaches force.
All these things are known about this organization. Anybody who wants to loiter and become part of one of its cells or part of its whole philosophy is, therefore, motivated by one reason alone-the notion of terror appeals to that person. It is as simple as that. Why doubts are expressed-and doubts that are pretty far off target and illogical-is beyond me. You could ask Jasper Cross-when he moved from Halifax to Montreal they came to call him James Cross-just what the FLQ is, and he would tell you. You could also have asked Mr. Laporte before he was murdered by the FLQ. I reject absolutely and out of hand any suggestion that clause 3 does not, in as specific a way as possible, represent what we in this Parliament are after, which is to come to grips with this terrorist organization. It is not a terrorist organization that was at work in czarist Russia or in the miserable thirties and forties in some European countries; it is one that is alive, very much alive, and at work in Canada today.
Public Order Act, 1970
I say that the definition contained in the bill is as reasonable an approach as a legal draftsman could make to identify the group that we are after. It must be effective, because several people have already pleaded guilty to being members of the FLQ and have been sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment. They must have known what they were about when they made that decision. I think there are safeguards. If somebody is picked up and wrongfully accused of association with the group, in due course a trial will be held and that person will be found not guilty.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
There may be a little oversensitivity because it does appear there is maladministration of the regulations under the War Measures Act. There is some question whether the rights of people are being respected by the police. But those things can be straightened out in time. Above all, what we have to consider now is that there is a problem to be met in Canada. That problem involves the rooting and stamping out of a terrorist organization. For those reasons, on behalf of the official opposition-I want to make that very clear, particularly to the people of the press-let me say we reject the amendment that is now proffered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the line taken today by the Creditiste members on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Roberval (M. Gauthier) is a symbolic gesture aimed at making the voice of the province of Quebec heard in the House on the problem now facing our country.
We wish our hon. colleagues and the Minister of Justice (M. Turner) to realize that the problem which has recently plagued a part of our province will probably go down in history as the "October events". This was not only a Quebec problem but a full-fledged Canadian national issue.
With patience and very often with impatience, I listened to the speeches of my colleagues of other parties. At times, I felt like rising to energetically protest against the insidious way of exaggerating the importance of problems in Quebec. In short, the intent was to present Quebecers as trouble makers, which is absolutely untrue.
My fellow citizens in Quebec want peace. They are against violence and the excessive use of force and that is why the mouthpiece of Quebec, the Ralliement Creditiste, sincerely supported the proclamation of the War Measures Act when the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) moved it at the height of the crisis. We gave our support in good faith because we were aware of the major problems facing Quebec.
Today, we are proud of having held out against anarchists and terrorists and those who want to overthrow the government by undemocratic methods.
Today, one month after the passage of the War Measures Act, one month after the death of a renowned Quebec statesman and the kidnapping of an equally

November 25, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
renowned British diplomat, we ask ourselves it the Prime Minister has not taken advantage of the tragic events in Quebec to make it look to other Canadians as a province not like the others which is difficult to control and which one day will have to be subdued, muzzled and put in its place once and for all, in order to restore peace.
It is a serene spirit that in the course of this debate today we wish to submit the following argument in connection with clause 3.
The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) said earlier that it was to please our colleagues of the New Democratic and Progressive Conservative parties that he had repeated in clause 3, by means of an amendment, what was stated in the preamble.
In doing so, he has displeased us much as he has repealed in clause 3 the provisions of the bill that we did not like.
The preamble stated that it was intended to declare illegal the association known as Le Front de Liberation du Quebec because it was a threat to public order. That is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, it means Quebec.
Besides, one can read, and I quote:
-who advocate the use of force or the commission of crime as a means of accomplishing governmental change within Canada with respect to the province of Quebec-
It does not concern the province of Ontario, British Columbia nor New Brunswick. It is clearly stated here twice that it is "with respect to the province of Quebec".
I go on quoting:
-or its relationship to Canada-
The War Measures Act was applied when the trouble started in order to settle once for all the problems in Quebec and to restore public order there.
The Creditistes unreservedly supported this act because these were major problems, because it was necessary to regain control of the situation, because we lacked information and because the right hon. Prime Minister could only say that there existed in Quebec a state of "apprehended insurrection".
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Today-as pointed out by my colleague from Champlain (Mr. Matte)-we are still wondering what that state of insurrection was? What were the motives, the reasons, the evidence, the assumptions on which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) could rely to say to the government of Quebec, to the city of Montreal, that there really was a state of insurrection in Quebec? I do not say there was not, but we are entitled to know the real reasons that made the application of the War Measures Act necessary, to maintain order in Quebec.
A month has gone by since that act was invoked, but we have neither saved the life of Pierre Laporte nor found James Richard Cross.
Does the state of insurrection still exist in Quebec?
Mr. Speaker, the game has been lost, as far as the War Measures Act is concerned, because the government did

not take the proper action. They panicked, created tension in Quebec and raised a national storm to show all Canada that they were justified in subduing Quebec once and for all. We are hurt, as Quebecers, to find the name of our province continuously coming up in the bill and to see that once more the problem is confined solely to Quebec.
A month has gone by since the War Measures Act was brought into force. However, at the time it was passed, it was fully agreed that it would remain in force only temporarily and that it would be replaced by permanent legislation in the near future. Instead of permanent legislation, the government is introducing another temporary measure to replace the first, on the grounds that there had not been time to draft a permanent one.
In all fairness, I must say that the Prime Minister sent a letter to all party leaders asking them for suggestions for the drafting of a permanent legislation. None of the suggestions made by the Creditists was accepted. Our leader made suggestions for the drafting of a permanent law, but they were disregarded.
The suggestions made by other party leaders were also brushed aside. In order to conceal its inaction, its incompetence, and to justify the dictatorial means used to subdue Quebec, the government told that province: We are applying the War Measures Act, we are bringing in the Army and we will do even better and act more sensibly once a permanent law is adopted. This legislation has not been introduced yet. It is quite possible that it will not be during this session. Since we have no guarantee that it will be introduced, we must be content with an inadequate and unfair legislation that repeat the mistake of the War Measures Act and applies only to Quebec.
This is what I find revolting as a Quebec federalist: an attempt to condemn an unlawful association in Quebec because it questions the status of the province of Quebec with regard to its relationship to Canada, implicitly means that the Canadian government uses the law to impose on Quebecers, regardless of their political party, the constitutional framework in which they must live. Under such a law, they are told: You are going to live under this set-up or you will be subject to convictions under the War Measures Act for the preservation of public order. And this, under the pretext that they are not using democratic means to achieve their purpose.
Agitation is not confined to Quebec and Quebec is not the only place where people are asking questions about the constitution. It is not only in Quebec that people resort to violence in desperation because of unemployment, misery and lack of welfare.
This bill deals with none of these problems but only calls the attention of Canadians to the problems of Quebec instead of striking at the root of terrorism in Quebec, which we deeply regret.
Instead of bearing down on the underlying causes of this evil, the government says: "We shall subdue you, break you, muzzle you! We shall even go as far as

making this legislation retroactive so as to reach all the trouble-makers who may have disturbed public order."
Mr. Speaker, we are saying that the government, in this respect, lacks good faith. And I wish to tell the hon. Minister of Justice and my colleagues that we from Quebec, while we strongly oppose violence, also oppose this government's misuse of power. We stand against violence and force. We supported the War Measures Act but we disapprove of this kind of provocation on the part of a government which, because of its inability to act is spreading poverty, hardship and despair among our people, to such an extent that this is unfortunately but the beginning of terrorism.
Mr. Speaker, there are twice as many university graduates as there are jobs available. What shall we do tomorrow with those young people? God knows.
Public Order Act, 1970
"frame" Quebec and refuses to admit that difficulties can exist elsewhere in Canada, not only does he fail to solve the problem, but he risks to bring about a revival of terrorism, violence and force.
When the first bombs exploded, the government was much alarmed. When they kept on exploding, the government did nothing. When the Company of Young Canadians started to pay its expenses out of the public funds the government did nothing. When Mr. Saulnier from Montreal came here and said to the government: It is time you acted in Quebec, that you came to the assistance of the City of Montreal to restore order, and that you stop financing the revolution in Quebec. The government answered: No, that is untrue, that is nonsense Saulnier is wrong.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, those young people are desperate, and the government, instead of coping with real problems, beguiles the people with supposedly severe crises, with war measures acts, or with the use of excessive powers, so that tomorrow, if the troubles go on, we will be told again that Quebec is the trouble-maker in confederation.
Mr. Speaker, this attitude is quite unjust and provoking to my fellow citizens of Quebec, who are not violent, who do not want to use force, but who want to have valid and reasonable motives for remaining within the Canadian confederation. As a Quebec federalist, it is difficult for me to make my fellow Quebecers understand that confederation is viable and that life within its framework is pleasant, when one sees a government provoke these people and take advantage of a crisis, no matter how minor, to show off its strength and give orders to its Quebec servant.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to conclude my remarks. We approve the strong measures to condemn revolutionaries and put some order in Quebec. We are prepared to support the government in its efforts to restore public order in Canada. However, we disagree when it wants to confine the problem to Quebec, and say very clearly in its bill that the problem of terrorism only exists in Quebec, for this is untrue.
When the government wants to make us believe through its bill that revolutionaries exist only in Quebec, this is also untrue, even though the minister states that this bill applies to the whole of Canada. But, if this is true, Mr. Speaker, as he is now suggesting by shaking his head, that he only deletes the expression "Province of Quebec", and that he no longer names the province of Quebec in this bill, then he will have our full support, as he had on the proclamation of the War Measures Act. But as long as he wants to confine the terrorists, the revolutionaries, the bearded ones and the trouble-makers to Quebec, we will not agree, because this is provoking for us, and unjust for the Quebecers. Mr. Speaker, we ask our colleagues from the other provinces to show for our problems the same broadness of mind we showed for theirs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the debate in Committee of the Whole and the debate on the amendments moved during the third reading stage of this bill. I listened with particular interest to the last speaker. He discussed one of the amendments in terms of the relationship of this bill to the province of Quebec. Most members have had to consider in the last few weeks the reluctance by members from the province of Quebec to make a decision or indicate to this House problems with which they are familiar; they were willing to shout across the floor of the chamber indicating that other members were not familiar with the problems.
I feel sorry for the people of Quebec. They have found their government wanting. The government of that province cannot conduct its ordinary affairs. The Quebec provincial police are wanting. There is no cohesion in the metropolitan police force of Montreal. There is no unity among those police forces. There are in this House approximately 75 representatives from the province of Quebec. I am sure in the last six weeks they have been very concerned about the problems in their province. However, many of those members have not done anything in the House other than to vote or speak from their seats. The people of Quebec must have been shocked when their government, which was elected only a short time ago, had to ask for federal police to deal with a police strike situation. I am sure they were not proud of the fact that federal troops had to be called in to deal with the problem of strike action. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) is willing to give great power to the Quebec system of justice. However, it has not operated in the normal sense that the citizens of the province expect.
I sympathize with the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin). He stated that as a member from Quebec it was his impression that this bill is directed entirely against his province. While the minister will say that is not correct, and I agree with him, it does indicate the feeling of most of the citizens of Quebec, namely, that this matter has been treated as a political problem. In the first place there was considered to be an insurrection. This legislation indicates that there was an apprehended insurrection in the province of Quebec. Everyone in the country now knows this is not true. The "minister of regional disparity" indicated that 3,000 or more persons m high places and elsewhere were involved in this insurrection. The Minister of Justice has had the full powers of our national police force and the police forces in the province of Quebec, as well as 6,000 or 7,000 troops. Thousands of raids were made which resulted in hundreds of arrests. The minister has now indicated that not more than 150 people are involved. Probably a lot less people than that are involved.
Most people feel that when the two Rose brothers, Simard and four or five other people are apprehended, the insurrection in Quebec will cease. If that is true, why are the members from Quebec not demanding that the

November 25, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
federal government help the province of Quebec to eliminate these problems? Obviously, Scotland Yard, Interpol, the United States police and international police forces are at the beck and call of the federal police in Canada. Not too long ago they received assistance from these police forces to help strengthen security in this country.
The members from Quebec should make this type of request to the federal government, rather than just participating in votes. They should do something positive and constructive. I have talked with a number of people from Quebec who are not interested in politics. They do not care about the political structure of Quebec or, for that matter, of Canada. Nevertheless, they are very proud of being citizens of Quebec, they are very proud of being citizens of Montreal and they are very ashamed that their police forces do not seem to be able to do the normal job of police operations which is expected in other places.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It is all very well for the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) to say that when 22 million Canadians are in danger of something, perhaps loss of liberty, it is time some people gave up a portion of their liberty so that the rest of the people could enjoy it. Mr. Speaker, every dictator in the world has always said: Give me power; I will only need it for a short time and I will clear up the mess and make it safe for you to walk in the streets. Dictators are always promising to make their countries safe by taking away the liberties of the people. This is not what Canad ans want. This, surely, is not what the people of Quebec want. I am shocked that the Quebec members should sit in their seats and, worse still, vote for anything the government presents to them.
There have not been many really strong people from the province of Quebec in the federal field, at least since I have been in this House. They come here to vote, not to put forward ideas. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Lotbiniere say this afternoon that as a Member of Parliament and as a citizen of Quebec he did not want Quebec to be treated differently from the other provinces. I am sure most of the people of Quebec are not looking for different treatment.
The legislation before us is repugnant to everyone who thinks about it. Some members are inclined to take the view: We are not in Quebec and this law will apply especially to Quebec. It will not hurt me or the people I represent, so we shall not do a damned thing about it; let us not worry about whether anyone else gets hurt. The people of Quebec will revolt eventually against the treatment they have received over the years. It is all very well for the "minister of regional disparity" to say that FRAP is a terrible organization, that it is part of the insurrection. This was one of the reasons for the implementation of the War Measures Act in the first place.
I was surprised when I first came to this House, because I was new and did not know much about these things, to note that the last time we used the War Measures Act we allowed Camillien Houde to get out of gaol and he was elected in Montreal with a huge majority.

Other Canadians were also surprised. But I was not surprised a few weeks ago when not one person was elected to the Montreal council in opposition to Mayor Drapeau.
Let us suppose the "minister of regional disparity" was right in assuming that some of the FRAP candidates were people who should not have been elected; I do not know. Can he tell me that there is not one person among those who stood for election from that party who would not have been suitable for office, who would not have had the good of the city at heart? Was it only the people who supported Mr. Drapeau who should have stood? After all, many of the things which have been done, or neglected, by the present administration of Montreal have not been especially advantageous to the people of that city. There are the slums, for example. There are many other social problems. But they could have Expo, which cost us $300 million, a sum we gladly donated to that cause. And Mayor Drapeau is now working to get the Olympics for Montreal. I said in this House that this would cost us $50 million, but one of my friends who knows something about sports said $50 million would not cover the expenses of the last two countries in which the games were held, so the cost to the Canadian people will probably be considerably more.

As usual, all members opposite do is make a noise. Most Canadians find Montreal an amusing city to visit, a city where things are a little different. It is also Canada's largest city; this is a fact which many of us do not realize. A city of two million inhabitants is not easily policed, no matter how good the police force may be. It is not unusual in a city of this size that there should be 60 or 70 murders a year.
In passing this legislation we are not doing a service to the people of Quebec. We may be doing a service to the government of Quebec or to the Mayor of Montreal. But the citizens of Montreal want to clean-up their city. They want to build a police force sufficiently trained to handle the terrorism which has been practiced by half a dozen young political terrorists bent on destroying the political institutions of the province. There are economic problems in Quebec which the representatives of that province have not brought to the attention of the House.
